business_impact: Odoo publishes a fixed support window for every version, and a migration scoped against a version already inside — or past — that window buys less runway than it looks like. The cost isn't only a second migration coming sooner; it's that a version past its own support date stops receiving security patches, which the earlier hazard content on this topic already covers for the source side. Here it applies to the destination: paying for a migration and landing on a version that itself needs replacing within a year is a scoping problem worth catching before the project starts, not after.
checklist_item: Confirm the migration target's own Odoo support window before scoping the project
name: Migration target itself is approaching or past end of support
recommendation: Where the target is "ending_soon", confirm the timeline against the current published end-of-support date and weigh whether the next major version is close enough to target instead — Odoo's annual release cadence means one is often within reach. Where the target is "unsupported", treat this as a hazard, not a data-entry check: nothing built or configured against an unsupported version will keep receiving security patches from the day it goes live. Re-scope to a currently supported version unless there is a specific, documented reason not to.
symptom: Partway through scoping a migration, the version being targeted turns out to be one Odoo is about to stop patching, or already has — so the project now under discussion would need to be repeated again in the near future rather than buying the usual multi-year runway.
symptom_queries: which odoo version should I migrate to
technical_explanation: Every Odoo version carries a fixed support end date, published by Odoo and re-verified annually against its own documentation (see versions/support_matrix.py's staleness guard). A migration project typically runs weeks to months from scoping to cutover, and the version it lands on then needs to remain viable for a further period — the whole point of migrating rather than staying put. Scoping against a version already inside its support window's final stretch, or one that has already passed its end date, compresses that runway without anyone having decided to accept a shorter one.

business_impact: A migration scoped against a target that isn't actually ahead of the current version produces a report with nothing real to say about upgrade risk, module compatibility or cutover steps — the questions a migration assessment exists to answer don't apply to "moving" to where the instance already is. Catching this before the assessment is written is cheaper than a client reading a report that doesn't match what they asked for.
checklist_item: Confirm the stated migration target is genuinely ahead of the running version
name: Stated migration target does not advance the instance forward
recommendation: Re-confirm which version the engagement is actually targeting and re-run the collection with the corrected --target-version. If the instance is genuinely already on the intended target, this is not a migration engagement and the migration-family checks and report section do not apply.
symptom: The version named as the migration target turns out to match the version already running, or an older one — so the plan as stated doesn't describe an upgrade at all, which usually means the target was entered the wrong way round or copied from the wrong engagement.
technical_explanation: odoo.instance discovers the running series (odoo_version) directly from the authenticated connection; target_version is whatever --target-version asserted for this collection, validated against support_matrix.yaml at the CLI boundary but not checked against the running version there, since the CLI has no instance to compare against until collection actually runs. This check is that comparison, made once the two are in the same evidence row.
